items.title: "A Very Special Episode" of Office Hours
items.author: Brent Ozar Unlimited
items.summary:
When we were kids, TV shows would introduce some episodes as "a very special episode," and it meant they were going to tackle a sensitive topic like a family member dying, or drugs, or something heavy. In this episode, I talk about AI and what's happening to tech careers.

Here's the link I talk about in the video: https://thorstenball.com/blog/2026/09/19/what-i-believe-about-the-future-of-software-development/

00:00 Start
03:56 Index Cobbler: Thorsten compares human coders to Italian shoemakers. Is hand-tuning an index or query destined to become a luxury craft, and if so, who will still pay for it?
06:53 DROP TABLE Optimist: What permissions, approvals, and blast-radius limits would you require before letting an AI agent make changes directly in a production database?
08:38 Second-League Sam: If people without enough tokens are temporarily pushed into a “second league,” what career advice would you give a DBA whose employer will not pay for capable AI tools?
11:52 Legacy System Whisperer: The article predicts a generation-long replacement of old software. Does that give SQL Server DBAs a long career runway, or trap them maintaining systems nobody wants to understand?
13:26 SSMS Widow: If the terminal and CLI tools are dying, what happens to SSMS, sqlcmd, and Azure Data Studio? Is Management Studio going to turn into a chat window with a query plan hidden somewhere behind it?
16:13 The One Percent: Thorsten says performance optimization only matters for the 1% of software that actually has users. Isn't that 1% exactly the stuff that lands on my SQL Server? Does this article make DBAs more valuable or less?
17:21 Compiled But Wrong: He says 900 lines of AI-written C compiled and ran first try, so tests are pointless. How many AI-generated queries have you seen that compiled fine, ran fine, and returned the wrong rows? Isn't SQL the poster child for 'it ran' not meaning 'it's right'?
20:41 ACID Reflux: How do you reconcile probabilistic AI-generated software with the deterministic guarantees we expect from transactions, constraints, and financial data?
21:50 Query Store Historian: If agents constantly rewrite queries and database code, how should we baseline performance and prove which generated change caused a regression?
23:33 Meat Proxy DBA: The article says engineers who merely feed tickets to agents will lose value. What work keeps a DBA from becoming a “meat proxy” for AI-generated scripts?
25:30 Leading Comma Karen: Thorsten says code style rules like 80 columns exist for humans and agents don't care. Does that mean the T-SQL formatting wars are finally over? Can I stop arguing about leading commas and just let the robot pick?
27:40 Schema Sommelier: If nobody designs schemas by hand anymore, who teaches the model what a good one looks like? Won't it just learn from every terrible EAV table and GUID clustered key on Stack Overflow?
29:20 Review Bombed: Thorsten Ball says code review is dead because humans can't find bugs in AI-generated code fast enough. Should I stop reviewing the T-SQL my developers' agents generate, or is the database the one place where somebody still needs to read the query before it hits production?
31:32 Wrong-Thing Wrangler: If most future bugs are really “you asked for the wrong thing” bugs, are DBAs about to spend more time validating requirements and less time tuning queries?
33:31 sp_BlitzAutopilot: sp_Blitz and sp_BlitzIndex have AI features now. Given what Thorsten says about nobody reading output anymore, is the next step letting the scripts just fix things themselves? Would you ever ship that?
